item.title: Seven Weeks Until the Next Shutdown Cliff: Congress Breaks for Recess With September 30 Unresolved
item.body:
Congress has left Washington for its traditional August recess without finishing the fiscal year 2027 spending bills, leaving lawmakers just seven weeks to strike a deal before government funding lapses again on September 30. The recess comes only months after a record 76-day partial shutdown at the Department of Homeland Security disrupted immigration enforcement operations, border staffing, and related federal services earlier this year.

## A Familiar Pattern Repeats

Every year, Congress is supposed to pass twelve separate appropriations bills to fund the federal government before the new fiscal year begins on October 1. In practice, lawmakers routinely fall behind schedule, relying on stopgap continuing resolutions or last-minute omnibus packages to avoid a lapse in funding. This year appears to be following that familiar pattern: with the House and Senate now out of session for several weeks, negotiators have limited floor time left to reconcile competing spending priorities between the two chambers before the deadline arrives.

Congressional aides describe the current standoff as centering on familiar sticking points — the overall size of discretionary spending, funding levels for border security and immigration enforcement agencies, and policy riders attached to individual bills. None of these disagreements are new, but they carry extra weight this year given how disruptive the last funding lapse turned out to be.

## Why the Last Shutdown Still Looms Large

Earlier this year, a funding impasse specifically affecting the Department of Homeland Security stretched to 76 days, becoming the longest shutdown on record for that agency. During the lapse, hundreds of thousands of federal employees were furloughed or required to work without pay, immigration courts and case processing slowed significantly, and routine agency functions were delayed for weeks after funding was eventually restored.

That experience has left both congressional leaders and federal agencies wary of a repeat. Agency officials have reportedly begun contingency planning earlier than usual this year, and some lawmakers have publicly floated the idea of a short-term continuing resolution to buy additional negotiating time past September 30, rather than risk another prolonged lapse. Whether such a stopgap can pass both chambers, however, remains an open question, since continuing resolutions themselves require bipartisan support and have occasionally become bargaining chips in broader funding disputes.

## What Happens When Recess Ends

When lawmakers return to Washington in September, they will have only a handful of legislative days before the fiscal year ends. Congressional leadership will need to decide whether to push for a full-year omnibus package, pass individual appropriations bills piecemeal, or rely once again on a short-term continuing resolution to prevent a lapse while talks continue. Each path carries tradeoffs: a rushed omnibus can invite criticism over process, piecemeal bills are time-consuming to pass individually, and repeated short-term patches have drawn frustration from members in both parties who argue the approach makes long-term planning difficult for federal agencies.

## The Stakes for Federal Operations and the Public

A funding lapse does not affect every part of government equally. Programs deemed essential, such as active-duty military operations, air traffic control, and law enforcement, typically continue, though employees may go unpaid until funding is restored. Other functions — including some regulatory reviews, permitting processes, and administrative services — can slow or pause entirely. Federal contractors, national parks, and agencies that rely heavily on discretionary funding are often among the most visibly affected during an extended lapse.

Economists and budget analysts have also noted that repeated shutdown threats carry costs beyond the furlough period itself, including delayed federal payments, reduced consumer and business confidence during periods of uncertainty, and administrative costs associated with winding down and restarting agency operations. The Congressional Budget Office and Government Accountability Office have both published analyses of prior shutdowns highlighting these lingering effects, which can persist for weeks after funding is restored.

## What to Watch in September

As the September 30 deadline approaches, key signals to watch will include whether appropriations committees release updated bill text before recess ends, whether leadership in either chamber signals openness to a short-term continuing resolution, and how the White House and congressional leaders characterize their opening negotiating positions. Given the scale of disruption caused by the prior 76-day shutdown, both sides have incentives to avoid a repeat — but with the same underlying disagreements still unresolved, the coming weeks will determine whether Congress can act before the clock runs out again.
